lead: A system is the part of the universe you choose to study. Everything outside it is the surroundings, and the boundary is the surface, real or imaginary, between them. The boundary decides what may cross: mass, heat, work, or none. Engineers use this choice to analyse an engine cylinder, a compressor, a pressure cooker, or a UPI server room. The same hardware can be a closed, open, or isolated system depending on where you draw the boundary.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for the macroscopic view, where bulk properties describe the system.

blocks.text: Pick a region in space or a fixed amount of matter. That region is the system. The surroundings are everything outside it that can interact with it. The boundary separates the two. The boundary may be the metal wall of a tank, the dashed surface around a turbine, or an imaginary surface drawn across a pipe.

Mass, heat and work cross only at the boundary. A boundary that lets nothing cross makes the system isolated. A boundary that lets heat cross is diathermic. A boundary that blocks heat is adiabatic. A boundary that cannot move is rigid, so it cannot transmit displacement work. A rigid boundary can still pass heat or shaft work.

The same physical object can be classified in more than one way when you move the boundary. A pressure cooker with the lid closed is a closed system. Draw the boundary around the cooker and the kitchen air, and the pair is isolated only if no heat, mass or work crosses the outer surface. In practice, the kitchen wall may pass heat, so the pair is not isolated.

Closed system (control mass): no mass crosses the boundary. Energy may cross as heat or work. A sealed piston–cylinder with gas is closed. The gas mass stays constant, but the piston can move and heat can enter.

Open system (control volume): mass and energy may cross. A compressor, a turbine, a radiator, and a human body are open systems. Some syllabi call an open system a control volume. The boundary is drawn around the device; water or air enters and leaves.
Isolated system: no mass, no heat, and no work crosses. A perfectly insulated rigid flask of gas is close to isolated. A truly isolated system is an ideal limit; real walls leak some heat.

blocks.where: m₁ is the initial mass in kg; m₂ is the final mass in kg; mₑ is the mass that leaves in kg. Add mass that enters if any.

blocks.text: Classification depends on the boundary. A tank with a valve open is open while mass leaves. Close the valve and draw the boundary inside the closed tank: it becomes closed. It is isolated only if heat and work are also blocked.

Boundary names describe what crosses. A rigid boundary cannot move, so it does no p dV work. It may still pass heat or electrical work. An adiabatic boundary passes no heat, but work may cross. A diathermic boundary allows heat. An isolated system has a boundary that blocks mass, heat and work.

Steady state is a running condition: at any fixed point, properties do not change with time. Mass and energy may still flow through an open system at steady state. A steady-flow compressor can have constant inlet and outlet values for hours. Steady state is not the same as thermodynamic equilibrium; equilibrium is covered in Chapter 1.4.
Work and heat are transfers, not properties. Their sign convention is fixed in Chapter 1.6. For this chapter, only ask: does the boundary allow the transfer? Use this table.

figure.caption: The top block is the chosen system; the three lower blocks classify it and the small notes say what may cross. Notice that a closed system still allows energy, while an isolated system blocks mass, heat and work.

spec.title: System and boundary
spec.aria: A block diagram classifies systems as closed with no mass crossing but energy allowed, open with mass and energy crossing, and isolated with no mass, heat or work crossing.

examples.question: A rigid tank holds 2.0 kg of air. A valve opens and 0.50 kg of air escapes while 30 kJ of heat leaves the tank. Take the tank as the system. Does mass cross the boundary? Does energy cross it? Is the system closed or open?
steps: System: the air inside the tank. Boundary: the tank inner wall plus the valve opening.
Initial mass m₁ = 2.0 kg. Mass that leaves mₑ = 0.50 kg. Final mass m₂ = m₁ − mₑ = 2.0 − 0.50 = 1.5 kg.
mₑ = 0.50 kg > 0, so mass crosses the boundary; 0.50 kg leaves.
Heat Q = 30 kJ leaves, so energy crosses the boundary as heat. The tank is rigid, so no displacement work is done.
Mass crosses, so the system is open (a control volume). It is not closed. It is not isolated because heat crosses.
examples.answer: The final mass is 1.5 kg, 0.50 kg of air crosses the boundary, 30 kJ of heat leaves, and the tank is an open system.
examples.check:
m1 = 2.0
me = 0.50
m2 = m1 - me
Q = 30.0
print(m2)
print(me)
print(Q)

traps: Closed is not isolated. A closed system can exchange heat and work; only an isolated system blocks both.
Open means mass crosses. It does not mean the flow is steady or that flow work must be calculated now.
Rigid does not mean adiabatic. A rigid tank can pass heat through its wall.
Steady state is not equilibrium. A steady-flow device can have gradients and still have constant readings at each point.
Do not call a system isolated just because it is sealed; heat can cross a metal wall.

quiz.q: Define system, surroundings and boundary in one line each.
quiz.a: System: the chosen region; surroundings: everything outside it; boundary: the surface between them.

quiz.q: Why can a closed system exchange energy but not mass?
quiz.a: Closed means no mass crosses by definition. Heat and work can still cross the boundary, so energy changes.
An open system with a chosen boundary through which mass may cross; some syllabi use the name for an open system.

quiz.q: A rigid tank holds 3.0 kg of air. A valve lets 1.0 kg out; 20 kJ of heat enters. Take the tank as the system. Does mass cross? Does energy cross? Open or closed?
quiz.a: Mass leaves: 1.0 kg > 0, so mass crosses. Heat 20 kJ enters, so energy crosses. Final mass is 3.0 − 1.0 = 2.0 kg. With mass crossing, it is open.

quiz.q: A closed system has an adiabatic boundary. Can its volume change? Can work cross? Explain.
quiz.a: Adiabatic blocks heat only. A moving piston can change volume and do p dV work. So work can cross; heat cannot.

quiz.q: A sealed metal flask is called isolated. A thermometer is pushed through the wall. Is it strictly isolated? What crosses?
quiz.a: No. The thermometer creates a path for heat, and the metal wall can pass heat. It is at best closed, not isolated.

quiz.q: Why is steady state not the same as equilibrium?
quiz.a: Steady state means properties at a fixed point do not change with time, but gradients and flows may exist. Equilibrium means no unbalanced driving force anywhere.

quiz.q: A rigid tank initially holds 3.0 kg of air. A valve adds 1.0 kg; no heat and no work cross. Does mass cross? Open or closed? What is the final mass?
quiz.a: Mass enters: 1.0 kg, so mass crosses. It is open while the valve is open. Final mass is 3.0 + 1.0 = 4.0 kg. It is not isolated while the valve is open.

beyond: Not for the exam. Engineers draw control volumes around a single turbine stage, a whole refrigerator, or a data-centre cooling loop to write energy balances. The same boundary habit appears in CFD, where each mesh cell is a small control volume. Modern courses link this to the Reynolds transport theorem and to open-system exergy.
